timing: No reliable timing — state programs are waitlisted (California since February 2026) or not yet launched; DOE only began the funding-reopening process in June 2026.
eligibility: Program design: household income below 80% of area median income for full rebates, 80-150% for partial. In practice: only whatever your state's energy office currently has open — most states have nothing open to new applicants today.
catches: REJECTED: no uniform national program is currently accepting applications — California's HEEHRA reached capacity and went to waitlist in February 2026.
DOE's June 2026 guidance explicitly bars using the restarted rebates to ditch fossil fuels for electric heating — directly undercutting the route's premise.
The route's '$50-$500 per appliance' has no currently-obtainable official source; it is aspirational for an average user today.
Even where programs exist, rebates require buying the appliance first — a discount, not income.

steps: Do NOT act on this route as a live offer — it is rejected pending real state-level availability.
If you still want to check: go to your state energy office's website (search '[your state] energy office' — use the .gov site) and look for Home Energy Rebates / HEAR program status.
Confirm the program is funded AND currently accepting applications in your state — a waitlist is not an open program.
Only then: confirm income eligibility (usually <=150% AMI), qualifying equipment list, and whether a participating contractor is required.
biggest_catch: The federal electric-appliance rebates exist on paper but are not obtainable for an average user today — California's program hit capacity and went to waitlist in February 2026, other states haven't launched, and DOE's June 2026 guidance bars using the restarted rebates to switch from fossil fuels to electric.
